items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "positive feedback"?
options: A mechanism in which a change causes responses that increase the change further, as in the release of oxytocin during childbirth.
A muscle or gland that carries out a response to restore the factor to its set point.
The ideal value of a physiological factor around which it is kept by homeostatic control.
A cell or organ that detects a stimulus, i.e. a change in a factor, and passes information to a coordinator.
items.answer: A mechanism in which a change causes responses that increase the change further, as in the release of oxytocin during childbirth.
items.markingKey: Positive feedback: a mechanism in which a change causes responses that increase the change further, as in the release of oxytocin during childbirth.

items.stem: Explain why it is important to keep the water potential of the blood constant.
items.answer: Changes in water potential of tissue fluid would cause cells to gain water by osmosis and burst, or lose water and shrink; cell metabolism depends on correct concentrations.
items.markingKey: osmosis into/out of cells [1]; cells burst/shrink or metabolism disrupted [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the core temperature of a mammal must be kept close to 37 °C.
items.answer: Enzymes work at an optimum; higher temperatures denature enzymes and lower temperatures reduce kinetic energy, so metabolic reactions would be slowed or stop.
items.markingKey: enzymes optimum [1]; denaturation / slow reactions [1] [2]

items.stem: Nadia, in Accra, experiences a situation in which the water potential of the blood falls during dehydration. Describe how negative feedback restores the normal value, naming the receptor, coordinator and effectors.
items.answer: Receptor: osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus; coordinator: the hypothalamus and posterior pituitary; effectors/response: collecting duct cells insert aquaporins in response to ADH and reabsorb more water; result: blood water potential rises back towards normal; once normal, the response is reduced (negative feedback).
items.markingKey: receptor [1]; coordinator [1]; effector response [1]; return to set point and response switched off [1] [4]

items.stem: Omar, in Cairo, experiences a situation in which core body temperature falls below 36.5 °C. Describe how negative feedback restores the normal value, naming the receptor, coordinator and effectors.
items.answer: Receptor: thermoreceptors in the hypothalamus and skin; coordinator: the hypothalamus; effectors/response: skeletal muscles shiver; arterioles in the skin constrict; hair erector muscles contract; metabolism increases; result: temperature rises back towards 37 °C; once normal, the response is reduced (negative feedback).
items.markingKey: receptor [1]; coordinator [1]; effector response [1]; return to set point and response switched off [1] [4]

items.stem: Jonas ran a half-marathon in Toronto on a hot day. Core body temperature rose from 37.1 °C to 38.9 °C during the race; Jonas lost about 1.7 dm³ of water as sweat. (a) Explain why core temperature rose during the race. (b) Explain why this is an example of negative feedback.
items.answer: (a) Muscle contraction requires much ATP from respiration; respiration is inefficient, releasing heat; heat production exceeded heat loss in hot conditions. (b) The rise in temperature is detected and responses act to lower it back to the set point; responses decrease as temperature returns to normal.
items.markingKey: (a) respiration releases heat [1]; production exceeds loss / hot air [1] [2] (b) response opposes change [1]; switched off near set point [1] [2]

items.stem: A person's core temperature rises to 38.5 °C. Which response would occur?
options: Vasodilation of arterioles supplying skin capillaries
items.answer: Vasodilation of arterioles supplying skin capillaries
items.markingKey: Increases heat loss by radiation.

items.stem: Chloe, in Lisbon, experiences a situation in which blood glucose concentration rises after a meal. Describe how negative feedback restores the normal value, naming the receptor, coordinator and effectors.
items.answer: Receptor: β cells in the islets of Langerhans; coordinator: the pancreas (islets); effectors/response: liver and muscle cells take up glucose and convert it to glycogen in response to insulin; result: blood glucose falls back to about 5 mmol dm⁻³; once normal, the response is reduced (negative feedback).
items.markingKey: receptor [1]; coordinator [1]; effector response [1]; return to set point and response switched off [1] [4]

items.stem: Zara, in Hanoi, experiences a situation in which core body temperature rises above 37.5 °C. Describe how negative feedback restores the normal value, naming the receptor, coordinator and effectors.
items.answer: Receptor: thermoreceptors in the hypothalamus; coordinator: the hypothalamus; effectors/response: sweat glands secrete more sweat; arterioles in the skin dilate; hair erector muscles relax; result: temperature falls back towards 37 °C; once normal, the response is reduced (negative feedback).
items.markingKey: receptor [1]; coordinator [1]; effector response [1]; return to set point and response switched off [1] [4]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "deamination"?
options: The filtration of blood under high pressure in the glomerulus, through the capillary endothelium, basement membrane and podocytes, into the Bowman's capsule.
The uptake of useful substances such as glucose, amino acids, ions and water from the filtrate back into the blood, mainly in the proximal convoluted tubule.
A cell of the inner wall of Bowman's capsule with foot-like processes that leave filtration slits.
The removal of the amine group from excess amino acids in the liver, forming ammonia, which is converted to urea.
items.answer: The removal of the amine group from excess amino acids in the liver, forming ammonia, which is converted to urea.
items.markingKey: Deamination: the removal of the amine group from excess amino acids in the liver, forming ammonia, which is converted to urea.

items.stem: Explain how glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule.
items.answer: Sodium–potassium pumps on the basal membrane actively remove Na⁺ from PCT cells, lowering Na⁺ concentration inside; Na⁺ diffuses in from filtrate via co-transporter proteins carrying glucose with it (facilitated diffusion); glucose diffuses out into blood through carriers.
items.markingKey: Na⁺ pumped out across basal membrane [1]; Na⁺ gradient [1]; co-transport of glucose [1]; glucose diffuses into blood [1] [4]

items.stem: Explain how the cells of the proximal convoluted tubule are adapted for reabsorption.
items.answer: Microvilli give a large surface area; many mitochondria provide ATP for active transport; many co-transporter proteins; tight junctions; close to capillaries.
items.markingKey: microvilli [1]; mitochondria [1]; carrier/co-transporter proteins [1] [3]

items.stem: Measurements on Diego, a healthy adult, gave: glomerular filtration rate 110 cm³ min⁻¹; urine production 0.7 cm³ min⁻¹; plasma glucose 5 mmol dm⁻³; urea concentration 0.3 g dm⁻³ in plasma and 15.5 g dm⁻³ in urine. Calculate the amount of glucose filtered per minute, in mmol, and state how much of it appears in the urine.
items.answer: 0.55 mmol min⁻¹; none appears in urine
items.markingKey: 110 cm³ × 5 mmol dm⁻³ ÷ 1000 = 0.55 mmol [1]; all reabsorbed / none in urine [1] [2]

items.stem: Measurements on Isla, a healthy adult, gave: glomerular filtration rate 110 cm³ min⁻¹; urine production 1.1 cm³ min⁻¹; plasma glucose 4.5 mmol dm⁻³; urea concentration 0.33 g dm⁻³ in plasma and 16.9 g dm⁻³ in urine. (a) Calculate how many times more concentrated urea is in the urine than in the plasma. (b) Calculate the amount of glucose filtered per minute, in mmol, and state how much of it appears in the urine.
items.answer: (a) 51 times (b) 0.495 mmol min⁻¹; none appears in urine
items.markingKey: (a) 16.9 ÷ 0.33 = 51 [1] (b) 110 cm³ × 4.5 mmol dm⁻³ ÷ 1000 = 0.495 mmol [1]; all reabsorbed / none in urine [1] [2]

items.stem: Measurements on Ravi, a healthy adult, gave: glomerular filtration rate 125 cm³ min⁻¹; urine production 0.8 cm³ min⁻¹; plasma glucose 5.5 mmol dm⁻³; urea concentration 0.35 g dm⁻³ in plasma and 22 g dm⁻³ in urine. (a) Calculate the volume of filtrate produced in 24 hours, in dm³. (b) Calculate the amount of glucose filtered per minute, in mmol, and state how much of it appears in the urine.
items.answer: (a) 180 dm³ (b) 0.688 mmol min⁻¹; none appears in urine
items.markingKey: (a) 125 × 60 × 24 = 180,000 cm³ [1] = 180 dm³ [1] [2] (b) 125 cm³ × 5.5 mmol dm⁻³ ÷ 1000 = 0.688 mmol [1]; all reabsorbed / none in urine [1] [2]

items.stem: A clinician in Mexico City is investigating the effect of a drug that inhibits the sodium–potassium pumps of the PCT cells on kidney function. (a) Describe the route taken by a molecule of urea from the blood in the glomerulus to the collecting duct. (b) Explain why proteins and red blood cells do not normally pass into the filtrate.
items.answer: (a) Through pores in the capillary endothelium, the basement membrane and between podocytes into the Bowman's capsule; along the PCT, loop of Henle and DCT into the collecting duct. (b) The basement membrane acts as a filter that holds back molecules with RMM above about 69 000 and cells; red cells are too large to pass the endothelial pores.
items.markingKey: (a) three filtration layers [1]; correct order of nephron regions [1] [2] (b) basement membrane filter [1]; size limit [1] [2]

items.stem: A clinician in Kuala Lumpur is investigating the effect of a drug that narrows the afferent arteriole on kidney function. (a) Predict and explain the effect of the drug. (b) Explain why proteins and red blood cells do not normally pass into the filtrate.
items.answer: (a) Glomerular blood pressure would fall, so the rate of ultrafiltration (GFR) would decrease and less urine would be produced; urea would build up in the blood. (b) The basement membrane acts as a filter that holds back molecules with RMM above about 69 000 and cells; red cells are too large to pass the endothelial pores.
items.markingKey: (a) lower hydrostatic pressure [1]; lower GFR [1]; consequence [1] [3] (b) basement membrane filter [1]; size limit [1] [2]

items.stem: Which substance is normally present in glomerular filtrate but absent from the urine of a healthy person?
items.answer: Glucose
items.markingKey: Glucose is filtered and then all reabsorbed in the PCT.

items.stem: The concentration of glucose in the filtrate in the Bowman's capsule is 5 mmol dm⁻³. What is its concentration in the filtrate at the end of the PCT in a healthy person?
items.answer: 0 mmol dm⁻³
items.markingKey: All glucose is reabsorbed in the PCT.

items.stem: Explain how the structure of the glomerulus and Bowman's capsule allows ultrafiltration.
items.answer: Wide afferent and narrow efferent arterioles create high hydrostatic pressure; fenestrated endothelium; basement membrane acts as filter; podocytes with filtration slits; water potential gradient favours filtration.
items.markingKey: pressure difference [1]; pores in endothelium [1]; basement membrane filter [1]; podocytes [1] [4]

items.stem: A table compares the composition of blood plasma, glomerular filtrate and urine. For amino acids: plasma — present; filtrate — present at the same concentration; urine — absent. Explain these observations.
items.answer: Filtered; all reabsorbed in the PCT by co-transport with Na⁺.
items.markingKey: filtered; all reabsorbed in the PCT by co-transport with Na⁺ [2]

items.stem: Describe the structure of a nephron and explain how ultrafiltration and selective reabsorption take place.
items.answer: Bowman's capsule with glomerulus; PCT; loop of Henle; DCT; collecting duct. Ultrafiltration: high pressure, afferent wider than efferent, endothelium pores, basement membrane, podocytes, filtrate composition. Selective reabsorption in PCT: microvilli, mitochondria, Na⁺/K⁺ pump on basal side, co-transport of glucose/amino acids, water by osmosis, all glucose reabsorbed.
items.markingKey: nephron regions [2]; ultrafiltration mechanism [2]; filtrate composition [1]; PCT adaptations [1]; co-transport mechanism [1]; water by osmosis [1] [8]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "osmoreceptor"?
options: The control of the water potential of the blood and body fluids.
The hairpin section of the nephron that creates a low water potential in the medulla by a countercurrent multiplier.
The final part of the nephron, passing through the medulla, where the water content of urine is adjusted under the control of ADH.
A cell in the hypothalamus that detects changes in the water potential of the blood.
items.answer: A cell in the hypothalamus that detects changes in the water potential of the blood.
items.markingKey: Osmoreceptor: a cell in the hypothalamus that detects changes in the water potential of the blood.

items.stem: Explain how ADH increases water reabsorption in the collecting duct.
items.answer: ADH binds to receptors on collecting duct cells; this activates adenylyl cyclase forming cAMP, which leads to phosphorylation and fusion of vesicles containing aquaporins with the luminal membrane; water moves by osmosis through aquaporins into the medulla (low water potential) and into the blood.
items.markingKey: binds receptor [1]; cAMP / phosphorylation [1]; aquaporin vesicles fuse [1]; osmosis into medulla/blood [1] [4]

items.stem: Explain how the loop of Henle produces a region of low water potential in the medulla.
items.answer: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are actively transported out of the thick ascending limb, which is impermeable to water; this lowers the water potential of the medulla tissue fluid; water leaves the descending limb by osmosis; the countercurrent arrangement builds up the gradient, greatest at the tip of the loop.
items.markingKey: active transport of ions out of ascending limb [1]; ascending limb impermeable [1]; water leaves descending limb [1]; countercurrent multiplier [1] [4]

items.stem: Daniel drank 1.5 dm³ of water at time 0 in a study in Cairo. The rate of urine production (cm³ min⁻¹) at 30-minute intervals was: 0 min: 1.2, 30 min: 5.1, 60 min: 11.8, 90 min: 11.8, 120 min: 5.1, 150 min: 1.7. Describe the changes in the rate of urine production.
items.answer: The rate rose from 1.2 cm³ min⁻¹ to a peak of 11.8 cm³ min⁻¹ at 60 min, then fell back towards the original rate.
items.markingKey: rise to peak with data [1]; fall [1] [2]

items.stem: Tariq drank 1 dm³ of water at time 0 in a study in Auckland. The rate of urine production (cm³ min⁻¹) at 30-minute intervals was: 0 min: 0.9, 30 min: 11.8, 60 min: 11.8, 90 min: 4.9, 120 min: 1.4, 150 min: 0.9. (a) Suggest why it took time for the rate of urine production to increase. (b) Calculate the percentage increase in urine production rate from 0 min to the peak.
items.answer: (a) Water must be absorbed from the gut into the blood; ADH already in the blood must be broken down; aquaporins must be removed from membranes. (b) 1211%
items.markingKey: (a) absorption time [1]; ADH removal / aquaporins removed [1] [2] (b) (11.8 − 0.9) ÷ 0.9 × 100 = 1211% [2]

items.stem: Kwame has a mutation in the gene for aquaporin-2. Kwame produces about 8 dm³ of dilute urine per day, compared with about 1.5 dm³ normally. (a) Explain why this condition causes a large volume of dilute urine. (b) Calculate how many times more urine than normal the person produces.
items.answer: (a) Collecting duct cells do not insert aquaporins into their membranes, so they remain impermeable to water; little water is reabsorbed by osmosis into the medulla. (b) 5.3 times
items.markingKey: (a) aquaporins not inserted [1]; low permeability [1]; less reabsorption [1] [3] (b) 8 ÷ 1.5 = 5.3 [1]

items.stem: Explain why desert mammals such as kangaroo rats have very long loops of Henle.
items.answer: A longer loop creates a steeper water potential gradient in the medulla, so more water can be reabsorbed from the collecting ducts by osmosis and very concentrated urine is produced.
items.markingKey: steeper gradient [1]; more water reabsorbed / concentrated urine [1] [2]

items.stem: Aisha drank 1.5 dm³ of water at time 0 in a study in Doha. The rate of urine production (cm³ min⁻¹) at 30-minute intervals was: 0 min: 1.1, 30 min: 10.5, 60 min: 10.5, 90 min: 4.6, 120 min: 1.6, 150 min: 1.1. (a) Describe the changes in the rate of urine production. (b) Calculate the percentage increase in urine production rate from 0 min to the peak.
items.answer: (a) The rate rose from 1.1 cm³ min⁻¹ to a peak of 10.5 cm³ min⁻¹ at 30 min, then fell back towards the original rate. (b) 855%

items.stem: Grace has central (cranial) diabetes insipidus, in which the posterior pituitary releases little ADH. Grace produces about 11 dm³ of dilute urine per day, compared with about 1.5 dm³ normally. (a) Explain why this condition causes a large volume of dilute urine. (b) Suggest whether a synthetic form of ADH would be an effective treatment. Explain your answer. (c) Calculate how many times more urine than normal the person produces.
items.answer: (a) Collecting duct cells do not insert aquaporins into their membranes, so they remain impermeable to water; little water is reabsorbed by osmosis into the medulla. (b) Giving synthetic ADH (desmopressin) would help, because the collecting ducts can still respond to it. (c) 7.3 times
items.markingKey: (a) aquaporins not inserted [1]; low permeability [1]; less reabsorption [1] [3] (b) correct decision [1]; reason [1] [2] (c) 11 ÷ 1.5 = 7.3 [1]

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "the synthesis of glucose from non-carbohydrate sources such as amino acids and glycerol"?
items.answer: Gluconeogenesis
items.markingKey: Gluconeogenesis: the synthesis of glucose from non-carbohydrate sources such as amino acids and glycerol.

items.stem: Explain how glucagon causes the release of glucose from a liver cell.
items.answer: Glucagon binds to a receptor on the liver cell membrane; this activates a G protein and adenylyl cyclase; ATP is converted to cAMP; cAMP activates protein kinase A, which starts an enzyme cascade activating glycogen phosphorylase; glycogen is broken down to glucose, which diffuses out of the cell.
items.markingKey: binds receptor [1]; adenylyl cyclase / cAMP [1]; protein kinase / cascade [1]; glycogen phosphorylase / glycogenolysis [1]; glucose leaves [1] [5]

items.stem: Explain why the cAMP cascade allows a small amount of glucagon to have a large effect.
items.answer: Each step activates many molecules of the next enzyme, so the signal is amplified: one glucagon molecule leads to the release of millions of glucose molecules.
items.markingKey: each enzyme activates many [1]; amplification [1] [2]

items.stem: In a liver cell, one activated glucagon receptor activates one adenylyl cyclase molecule, which starts a cascade: each activated adenylyl cyclase makes 10 cAMP molecules; each cAMP leads to activation of 20 protein kinase molecules; each protein kinase activates 20 phosphorylase kinase molecules. How many molecules are activated at the last step for each glucagon receptor activated?

In a liver cell, one activated glucagon receptor activates one adenylyl cyclase molecule, which starts a cascade: each activated adenylyl cyclase makes 20 cAMP molecules; each cAMP leads to activation of 10 protein kinase molecules; each protein kinase activates 10 phosphorylase kinase molecules; each phosphorylase kinase activates 50 glycogen phosphorylase molecules. Each active glycogen phosphorylase releases 100 glucose molecules per second. Calculate the number of glucose molecules released per second for each glucagon receptor activated, and explain the advantage of this mechanism.
items.answer: 10,000,000 (= 1.0 × 10⁷); a small hormone signal gives a large, rapid response (amplification).
items.markingKey: 20 × 10 × 10 × 50 × 100 [1] = 10,000,000 [1]; amplification / fast large response [1] [3]

items.stem: In a liver cell, one activated glucagon receptor activates one adenylyl cyclase molecule, which starts a cascade: each activated adenylyl cyclase makes 50 cAMP molecules; each cAMP leads to activation of 50 protein kinase molecules. Each active glycogen phosphorylase releases 1000 glucose molecules per second. Calculate the number of glucose molecules released per second for each glucagon receptor activated, and explain the advantage of this mechanism.
items.answer: 2,500,000 (= 2.5 × 10⁶); a small hormone signal gives a large, rapid response (amplification).
items.markingKey: 50 × 50 × 1000 [1] = 2,500,000 [1]; amplification / fast large response [1] [3]

items.stem: In a glucose tolerance test, Aisha and Felix fasted overnight and then drank 75 g of glucose. Blood glucose (mmol dm⁻³) at 0, 30, 60, 90 and 120 min was: Aisha: 4.6, 8.4, 6.5, 5.1, 4.8; Felix: 8.3, 12.4, 14.6, 13.8, 11.1. (a) Calculate the percentage increase in blood glucose of Aisha from 0 to 30 minutes. (b) Explain why people with diabetes may use a biosensor rather than urine test strips to monitor their glucose.
items.answer: (a) 83% (b) Biosensors measure the current blood concentration quantitatively; urine strips only show glucose once the renal threshold is exceeded and reflect earlier levels.
items.markingKey: (a) (8.4 − 4.6) ÷ 4.6 × 100 = 83% [2] (b) blood vs urine / current value [1]; quantitative [1] [2]

items.stem: In a glucose tolerance test, Isla and Grace fasted overnight and then drank 75 g of glucose. Blood glucose (mmol dm⁻³) at 0, 30, 60, 90 and 120 min was: Isla: 4.7, 7.6, 6.4, 5.5, 5.2; Grace: 8, 13.9, 15, 14.1, 11.8. (a) Distinguish between type 1 and type 2 diabetes. (b) Calculate the percentage increase in blood glucose of Isla from 0 to 30 minutes.
items.answer: (a) Type 1: β cells destroyed (autoimmune), no insulin made, treated with insulin injections. Type 2: insulin produced but target cells less responsive (insulin resistance), linked to obesity, treated with diet/exercise/drugs. (b) 62%

items.stem: Which cells secrete glucagon?
options: α cells of the islets of Langerhans
β cells of the islets of Langerhans
items.answer: α cells of the islets of Langerhans
items.markingKey: α cells → glucagon; β cells → insulin.

items.stem: Explain how a glucose test strip detects glucose in urine.
items.answer: Glucose oxidase converts glucose (and oxygen) to gluconic acid and hydrogen peroxide; peroxidase uses the hydrogen peroxide to oxidise a colourless chromogen to a coloured compound; colour intensity is compared with a chart.
items.markingKey: glucose oxidase [1]; H₂O₂ produced [1]; peroxidase and chromogen colour [1]; compared with chart [1] [4]

items.stem: In a liver cell, one activated glucagon receptor activates one adenylyl cyclase molecule, which starts a cascade: each activated adenylyl cyclase makes 10 cAMP molecules; each cAMP leads to activation of 10 protein kinase molecules; each protein kinase activates 20 phosphorylase kinase molecules; each phosphorylase kinase activates 10 glycogen phosphorylase molecules. How many molecules are activated at the last step for each glucagon receptor activated?

Yusuf made a calibration curve for glucose using a glucose oxidase–peroxidase reagent, which forms a coloured product, and a colorimeter. Absorbance values for glucose standards (mmol dm⁻³): 0: 0.02, 2: 0.22, 4: 0.41, 6: 0.57, 8: 0.73, 10: 0.86. A fasting blood plasma sample treated in the same way gave an absorbance of 0.46. Suggest why reagents containing glucose oxidase are preferred to Benedict's solution for measuring glucose in blood or urine.
items.answer: They are specific for glucose (other reducing sugars do not react), quick, do not require heating and are portable.
items.markingKey: specific [1]; quick / no heating [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how the concentration of glucose in the blood is controlled, including the role of the second messenger cAMP.
items.answer: Set point ~5 mmol dm⁻³; detected by α and β cells of islets; insulin from β cells: GLUT4 vesicles, glycogenesis, respiration, fat; glucagon from α cells binds liver receptors; G protein; adenylyl cyclase; cAMP; protein kinase A cascade; glycogen phosphorylase; glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis; amplification; negative feedback.
items.markingKey: detection by islet cells [1]; insulin effects [2]; glucagon receptor and G protein [1]; cAMP and kinase cascade [2]; glucagon effects [1]; negative feedback [1] [8]

items.stem: Which term is defined as "a plant hormone (ABA) produced in response to water stress that causes stomata to close"?
items.answer: Abscisic acid
items.markingKey: Abscisic acid: a plant hormone (ABA) produced in response to water stress that causes stomata to close.

items.stem: Which ion moves into guard cells when stomata open?
items.answer: Potassium ions
items.markingKey: K⁺ influx lowers water potential so water enters.

items.stem: Explain how stomata open.
items.answer: In light, proton pumps in guard cell membranes use ATP to pump H⁺ out; this creates an electrochemical gradient; K⁺ channels open and K⁺ enters; malate is made from starch; water potential falls; water enters by osmosis; guard cells become turgid and bend apart.
items.markingKey: proton pumping [1]; K⁺ enter [1]; water potential falls, osmosis [1]; turgid guard cells curve / wall structure [1] [4]

items.stem: Leila floated epidermal strips from a broad bean leaf on solutions of different ABA concentrations in bright light for 1 hour, then measured the stomatal aperture of 10 stomata using an eyepiece graticule. Results table. ABA concentration / μmol dm⁻³: 0, 0.5, 2, 8, 32. Mean stomatal aperture / μm, trial 1: 11.9, 9.7, 7.6, 5.1, 3.3; trial 2: 11.5, 9.7, 7.3, 5.1, 3.2; trial 3: 11, 9.4, 7.9, 5, 3.1. Describe the trend shown by the results.
items.answer: As the ABA concentration increases, the mean stomatal aperture decreases (from 11.47 to 3.2).
items.markingKey: correct overall pattern [1]; data quoted with units / turning point given [1] [2]

items.stem: During a drought in a farming region near Lisbon, the ABA concentration in the xylem sap of sorghum plants rose about 23-fold before any wilting was seen. (a) Suggest a disadvantage to the plants of the response. (b) Describe the role of calcium ions in the response of guard cells to ABA.
items.answer: (a) CO₂ uptake falls so photosynthesis and growth (yield) decrease; leaves may overheat with less evaporative cooling. (b) Ca²⁺ act as a second messenger; they enter the cytoplasm (from outside and from vacuole) and open anion and K⁺ channels and inhibit H⁺ pumps.
items.markingKey: (a) less CO₂ / photosynthesis [1]; reduced yield / overheating [1] [2] (b) second messenger [1]; effect on channels [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how abscisic acid causes stomata to close.
items.answer: ABA binds to receptors on guard cell membranes; Ca²⁺ enters the cytoplasm and acts as a second messenger; this opens channels so K⁺ (and anions) leave and inhibits proton pumps; water potential of guard cells rises; water leaves by osmosis; cells become flaccid and the pore closes.
items.markingKey: ABA receptor [1]; Ca²⁺ second messenger [1]; K⁺ leave [1]; water leaves, flaccid [1] [4]

items.stem: Which structure acts as the coordinator in the control of body temperature?
items.answer: Hypothalamus
items.markingKey: The hypothalamus contains the thermoregulatory centre.

items.stem: Describe how negative feedback keeps a factor within narrow limits.
items.answer: A receptor detects a deviation from the set point; the coordinator sends signals to effectors; the effectors reverse the change; once normal, the stimulus is removed and the response stops.
items.markingKey: receptor detects change [1]; effector response reverses it [1]; response switched off when normal [1] [3]

items.stem: Arjun, in Doha, experiences a situation in which blood carbon dioxide concentration rises during exercise. Describe how negative feedback restores the normal value, naming the receptor, coordinator and effectors.
items.answer: Receptor: chemoreceptors in the medulla and the carotid and aortic bodies; coordinator: the breathing centre in the medulla; effectors/response: intercostal muscles and diaphragm contract faster and more strongly; result: CO₂ concentration falls back to normal; once normal, the response is reduced (negative feedback).
items.markingKey: receptor [1]; coordinator [1]; effector response [1]; return to set point and response switched off [1] [4]

items.stem: Felix ran a half-marathon in Kathmandu on a hot day. Core body temperature rose from 36.9 °C to 38.6 °C during the race; Felix lost about 2 dm³ of water as sweat. (a) Explain why core temperature rose during the race. (b) Describe the responses that increase heat loss from the skin. (c) Calculate the rise in core temperature as a percentage of the starting value.
items.answer: (a) Muscle contraction requires much ATP from respiration; respiration is inefficient, releasing heat; heat production exceeded heat loss in hot conditions. (b) Vasodilation of arterioles in the skin so more blood flows near the surface and loses heat by radiation; sweating, heat lost as sweat evaporates; hair erector muscles relax. (c) 4.6%
items.markingKey: (a) respiration releases heat [1]; production exceeds loss / hot air [1] [2] (b) vasodilation [1]; sweating / evaporation [1]; hairs flat [1] [3] (c) (38.6 − 36.9) ÷ 36.9 × 100 = 4.6% [1]

items.stem: Which substance is normally absent from glomerular filtrate?
items.answer: Plasma proteins such as albumin
items.markingKey: Proteins with RMM above about 69 000 are too large to pass the basement membrane.

items.stem: Explain why the concentration of urea in the filtrate increases along the nephron.
items.answer: Urea is not actively reabsorbed (only some diffuses back), while large volumes of water are reabsorbed from the filtrate, so the urea is concentrated.
items.markingKey: water reabsorbed [1]; urea mostly not reabsorbed [1] [2]

items.stem: Measurements on Mohammed, a healthy adult, gave: glomerular filtration rate 120 cm³ min⁻¹; urine production 1.3 cm³ min⁻¹; plasma glucose 4.5 mmol dm⁻³; urea concentration 0.27 g dm⁻³ in plasma and 18.5 g dm⁻³ in urine. Explain why the urea concentration in the urine is much higher than in the plasma.
items.answer: Most of the water in the filtrate is reabsorbed but most urea is not, so urea becomes concentrated.
items.markingKey: water reabsorbed [1]; urea retained [1] [2]

items.stem: A table compares the composition of blood plasma, glomerular filtrate and urine. For sodium ions: plasma — present; filtrate — present at the same concentration; urine — present at variable concentration. Explain these observations.
items.answer: Filtered; most reabsorbed by active transport, amount adjusted in the DCT and collecting duct.
items.markingKey: filtered; most reabsorbed by active transport, amount adjusted in the DCT and collecting duct [2]

items.stem: Explain how urea is formed and removed from the body.
items.answer: Excess amino acids deaminated in liver; amine group → ammonia; ammonia + CO₂ → urea in ornithine cycle; urea into blood; filtered in glomerulus; not reabsorbed (mostly); concentrated as water reabsorbed; stored in bladder and removed in urine.
items.markingKey: deamination [2]; ornithine cycle [1]; transport in blood [1]; ultrafiltration [1]; concentration in nephron [1] [6]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "aquaporin"?
options: The hairpin section of the nephron that creates a low water potential in the medulla by a countercurrent multiplier.
A channel protein in a membrane that allows water molecules to pass through rapidly.
A cell in the hypothalamus that detects changes in the water potential of the blood.
The final part of the nephron, passing through the medulla, where the water content of urine is adjusted under the control of ADH.
items.answer: A channel protein in a membrane that allows water molecules to pass through rapidly.
items.markingKey: Aquaporin: a channel protein in a membrane that allows water molecules to pass through rapidly.

items.stem: Explain what happens to ADH secretion and urine production after a person drinks a large volume of water.
items.answer: Blood water potential rises; osmoreceptors detect the rise; less ADH released; aquaporins removed from collecting duct membranes by endocytosis; less water reabsorbed; large volume of dilute urine.
items.markingKey: water potential rises [1]; less ADH [1]; fewer aquaporins [1]; more dilute urine [1] [4]

items.stem: Ravi drank 1.5 dm³ of water at time 0 in a study in Kathmandu. The rate of urine production (cm³ min⁻¹) at 30-minute intervals was: 0 min: 1.2, 30 min: 10.8, 60 min: 10.8, 90 min: 4.7, 120 min: 1.7, 150 min: 1.2. Calculate the percentage increase in urine production rate from 0 min to the peak.
Explain why insulin and glucagon are said to be antagonistic.
items.answer: They have opposite effects on blood glucose: insulin lowers it and glucagon raises it; the balance between them keeps blood glucose within narrow limits.
items.markingKey: opposite effects [1]; balance controls concentration [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how a biosensor measures the blood glucose concentration of a person with diabetes.
items.answer: Glucose oxidase immobilised on an electrode oxidises glucose; the reaction produces a small electric current proportional to glucose concentration, which is read on a digital display.
items.markingKey: immobilised glucose oxidase [1]; current proportional to concentration [1] [2]

items.stem: In a liver cell, one activated glucagon receptor activates one adenylyl cyclase molecule, which starts a cascade: each activated adenylyl cyclase makes 20 cAMP molecules; each cAMP leads to activation of 100 protein kinase molecules. How many molecules are activated at the last step for each glucagon receptor activated?

Sipho made a calibration curve for glucose using a glucose oxidase–peroxidase reagent, which forms a coloured product, and a colorimeter. Absorbance values for glucose standards (mmol dm⁻³): 0: 0.02, 2: 0.2, 4: 0.37, 6: 0.52, 8: 0.65, 10: 0.77. A fasting blood plasma sample treated in the same way gave an absorbance of 0.67. (a) Use the data to estimate the glucose concentration of the sample. (b) State whether this person's blood glucose concentration is within the normal fasting range. Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) 8.3 mmol dm⁻³ (b) No: it is above the normal range of about 4–6 mmol dm⁻³ (hyperglycaemia), which may indicate diabetes.
items.markingKey: (a) between 8 and 10 mmol dm⁻³ [1]; interpolation gives 8.3 mmol dm⁻³ (± 0.2) [1] [2] (b) correct comparison with 4–6 mmol dm⁻³ [1]

items.stem: Describe how glucose can be measured in urine and in blood, and explain why measurements are important for people with diabetes.
items.answer: Dip sticks: glucose oxidase + peroxidase + chromogen; colour chart; semi-quantitative. Biosensor: glucose oxidase on electrode, current, digital readout; blood sample. Importance: adjust insulin dose/diet, avoid hypoglycaemia and hyperglycaemia, long-term damage.
items.markingKey: dip stick chemistry [2]; colour chart [1]; biosensor [2]; importance [1] [6]

items.stem: Epidermal strips are placed in a solution containing ABA in bright light. What happens to the guard cells?
options: They gain K⁺ and the stomata open
They lose K⁺ and water and the stomata close
items.answer: They lose K⁺ and water and the stomata close
items.markingKey: ABA triggers Ca²⁺ signalling and K⁺ efflux.

items.stem: Mohammed floated epidermal strips from a broad bean leaf on solutions of different ABA concentrations in bright light for 1 hour, then measured the stomatal aperture of 10 stomata using an eyepiece graticule. Results table. ABA concentration / μmol dm⁻³: 0, 0.5, 2, 8, 32. Mean stomatal aperture / μm, trial 1: 12.2, 10.6, 7.4, 4.9, 3.2; trial 2: 12.5, 10.7, 7.8, 5.3, 3.4; trial 3: 12.5, 9.9, 11.5, 5.3, 3.3. State the type of graph you would draw to display these results and what you would plot on each axis.
items.answer: A line graph: ABA concentration on the x-axis and mean mean stomatal aperture on the y-axis.
items.markingKey: line graph (continuous independent variable) [1]; ABA concentration on x-axis and mean stomatal aperture on y-axis [1] [2]

items.stem: Hana floated epidermal strips from a broad bean leaf on solutions of different ABA concentrations in bright light for 1 hour, then measured the stomatal aperture of 10 stomata using an eyepiece graticule. Results table. ABA concentration / μmol dm⁻³: 0, 0.5, 2, 8, 32. Mean stomatal aperture / μm, trial 1: 12, 10.4, 7.7, 5.1, 3.3; trial 2: 12.1, 10.2, 7.7, 5.2, 3.4; trial 3: 13, 10.6, 4.6, 5.5, 3.4. (a) State two variables that should be kept constant in this investigation. (b) Explain the results.
items.answer: (a) Light intensity; temperature. (b) ABA binds to receptors on guard cells, causing Ca²⁺ to enter and K⁺ to leave, so water leaves by osmosis and the guard cells become flaccid; higher concentrations bind more receptors so more stomata close.
items.markingKey: (a) Any two from: light intensity; temperature; age and position of the leaf; time on the solution; concentration of K⁺ in the solution [2] (b) ABA receptor [1]; K⁺ loss / Ca²⁺ [1]; water out, flaccid guard cells [1] [3]

items.stem: Which is an example of negative feedback?
options: A fall in blood glucose causes glucagon secretion, which raises blood glucose
Blood clotting factors activate more clotting factors
An action potential opens more sodium channels
Oxytocin release increases uterine contractions, causing more oxytocin release
items.answer: A fall in blood glucose causes glucagon secretion, which raises blood glucose
items.markingKey: The response reverses the change.

items.stem: Which describes positive feedback?
options: A change triggers a response that reverses it
A change triggers a response that increases the change further
A factor remains at its set point
items.answer: A change triggers a response that increases the change further
items.markingKey: e.g. oxytocin in childbirth.

items.stem: Tomás, in Madrid, experiences a situation in which blood glucose concentration falls during exercise. Describe how negative feedback restores the normal value, naming the receptor, coordinator and effectors.
items.answer: Receptor: α cells in the islets of Langerhans; coordinator: the pancreas (islets); effectors/response: liver cells break down glycogen to glucose (glycogenolysis) and make glucose by gluconeogenesis in response to glucagon; result: blood glucose rises back to about 5 mmol dm⁻³; once normal, the response is reduced (negative feedback).
items.markingKey: receptor [1]; coordinator [1]; effector response [1]; return to set point and response switched off [1] [4]

items.stem: Elena ran a half-marathon in Kuala Lumpur on a hot day. Core body temperature rose from 36.9 °C to 39 °C during the race; Elena lost about 1.5 dm³ of water as sweat. (a) Explain why core temperature rose during the race. (b) Describe the responses that increase heat loss from the skin. (c) Calculate the rise in core temperature as a percentage of the starting value.
items.answer: (a) Muscle contraction requires much ATP from respiration; respiration is inefficient, releasing heat; heat production exceeded heat loss in hot conditions. (b) Vasodilation of arterioles in the skin so more blood flows near the surface and loses heat by radiation; sweating, heat lost as sweat evaporates; hair erector muscles relax. (c) 5.7%
items.markingKey: (a) respiration releases heat [1]; production exceeds loss / hot air [1] [2] (b) vasodilation [1]; sweating / evaporation [1]; hairs flat [1] [3] (c) (39 − 36.9) ÷ 36.9 × 100 = 5.7% [1]

items.stem: Why is blood pressure in the glomerulus high?
options: The efferent arteriole is wider than the afferent arteriole
The efferent arteriole has a smaller diameter than the afferent arteriole
The glomerulus is close to the heart
items.answer: The efferent arteriole has a smaller diameter than the afferent arteriole
items.markingKey: Narrow efferent arteriole builds up hydrostatic pressure.

items.stem: Explain why glucose appears in the urine of a person with untreated diabetes.
items.answer: Blood glucose concentration is so high that the filtrate contains more glucose than the co-transporters in the PCT can reabsorb; the carriers are saturated so excess glucose stays in the filtrate.
items.markingKey: high blood/filtrate glucose [1]; carriers saturated [1] [2]

items.stem: A table compares the composition of blood plasma, glomerular filtrate and urine. For red blood cells: plasma — present; filtrate — absent; urine — absent. Explain these observations.
items.answer: Cells are far too large to pass through the endothelium and basement membrane.
items.markingKey: cells are far too large to pass through the endothelium and basement membrane [2]

items.stem: Measurements on Elena, a healthy adult, gave: glomerular filtration rate 110 cm³ min⁻¹; urine production 2 cm³ min⁻¹; plasma glucose 4.5 mmol dm⁻³; urea concentration 0.26 g dm⁻³ in plasma and 24.2 g dm⁻³ in urine. Calculate the percentage of the filtered water that is reabsorbed.

A clinician in Colombo is investigating the effect of a drug that inhibits the sodium–potassium pumps of the PCT cells on kidney function. (a) Describe the route taken by a molecule of urea from the blood in the glomerulus to the collecting duct. (b) Explain why the PCT cells contain many mitochondria. (c) Explain why the hydrostatic pressure in the glomerular capillaries is high.
items.answer: (a) Through pores in the capillary endothelium, the basement membrane and between podocytes into the Bowman's capsule; along the PCT, loop of Henle and DCT into the collecting duct. (b) They provide ATP for active transport of Na⁺ out of the cells by the Na⁺/K⁺ pumps, which drives co-transport of glucose and amino acids. (c) The efferent arteriole is narrower than the afferent arteriole and the glomerulus receives blood from the renal artery at high pressure.
items.markingKey: (a) three filtration layers [1]; correct order of nephron regions [1] [2] (b) ATP for active transport [1]; Na⁺ gradient for co-transport [1] [2] (c) The efferent arteriole is narrower than the afferent arteriole and the glomerulus receives blood from the renal artery at high pressure [2] [2]

items.stem: Name the second messenger that is produced when ADH binds to receptors on collecting duct cells.
items.answer: Cyclic AMP (cAMP).
items.markingKey: Cyclic AMP (cAMP) [1]

items.stem: Ravi says: "ADH is made by the posterior pituitary gland." Explain whether Ravi is correct.
items.answer: ADH is made by neurosecretory cells in the hypothalamus and stored in and released from the posterior pituitary.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: ADH is made by neurosecretory cells in the hypothalamus and stored in and released from the posterior pituitary. [2]

Mei writes in a revision note: "Glucagon is the same as glycogen." Identify the error and write a correct statement.
items.answer: Glucagon is a peptide hormone that raises blood glucose; glycogen is a polysaccharide store.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Glucagon is a peptide hormone that raises blood glucose; glycogen is a polysaccharide store. [2]

items.stem: Zara writes in a revision note: "Glucagon enters the liver cell and breaks down glycogen." Identify the error and write a correct statement.
items.answer: Glucagon binds to a receptor on the cell surface membrane; the signal is passed on by cAMP to enzymes inside the cell.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Glucagon binds to a receptor on the cell surface membrane; the signal is passed on by cAMP to enzymes inside the cell. [2]

items.answer: No: it is below the normal range (hypoglycaemia).

items.stem: In a liver cell, one activated glucagon receptor activates one adenylyl cyclase molecule, which starts a cascade: each activated adenylyl cyclase makes 20 cAMP molecules; each cAMP leads to activation of 10 protein kinase molecules; each protein kinase activates 20 phosphorylase kinase molecules. Each active glycogen phosphorylase releases 2000 glucose molecules per second. Calculate the number of glucose molecules released per second for each glucagon receptor activated, and explain the advantage of this mechanism.
items.answer: 8,000,000 (= 8.0 × 10⁶); a small hormone signal gives a large, rapid response (amplification).
items.markingKey: 20 × 10 × 20 × 2000 [1] = 8,000,000 [1]; amplification / fast large response [1] [3]

items.stem: In a glucose tolerance test, Mohammed and Ines fasted overnight and then drank 75 g of glucose. Blood glucose (mmol dm⁻³) at 0, 30, 60, 90 and 120 min was: Mohammed: 5.1, 8.5, 6.2, 5.4, 4.8; Ines: 7.7, 12, 14.2, 13.9, 11.3. (a) Explain the changes in the blood glucose of Mohammed between 30 and 120 minutes. (b) Explain why people with diabetes may use a biosensor rather than urine test strips to monitor their glucose.
items.answer: (a) Rise detected by β cells; insulin secreted; liver and muscle cells take up glucose (GLUT4), convert to glycogen and respire more; blood glucose returns to normal by 120 min. (b) Biosensors measure the current blood concentration quantitatively; urine strips only show glucose once the renal threshold is exceeded and reflect earlier levels.
items.markingKey: (a) β cells / insulin [1]; uptake by cells / GLUT4 [1]; glycogenesis [1]; data quoted [1] [4] (b) blood vs urine / current value [1]; quantitative [1] [2]

items.stem: Why do stomata usually open in the light?
options: Light heats the guard cells so they expand
Light causes guard cells to lose water
Proton pumping leads to K⁺ uptake, lowering the water potential of guard cells
Light breaks down ABA in the roots
items.answer: Proton pumping leads to K⁺ uptake, lowering the water potential of guard cells
items.markingKey: Water enters by osmosis; turgid cells open the pore.

items.stem: During a drought in a farming region near Manila, the ABA concentration in the xylem sap of cotton plants rose about 40-fold before any wilting was seen. (a) Explain how this rise in ABA would help the plants survive the drought. (b) Suggest a disadvantage to the plants of the response.
items.answer: (a) ABA travels to leaves and binds to guard cell receptors; stomata close; transpiration falls so water is conserved. (b) CO₂ uptake falls so photosynthesis and growth (yield) decrease; leaves may overheat with less evaporative cooling.
items.markingKey: (a) ABA to leaves [1]; stomata close [1]; less transpiration [1] [3] (b) less CO₂ / photosynthesis [1]; reduced yield / overheating [1] [2]
